brief.role: Core surgical trainee on the trauma team
brief.scenario: Mr Lewis Everleigh, 34, came off his motorcycle at speed 40 minutes ago. He has severe pelvic pain. HR 128, BP 82/50. The paramedics have not applied a pelvic binder.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on his immediate management. His response to treatment will be given to you as you go.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Stop the bleeding while you assess: binder, blood, tranexamic acid, then let his response decide CT or haemorrhage control.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Sending a non-responder to CT, or placing the binder over the iliac crests.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Catastrophic haemorrhage first: a pelvic binder at the greater trochanters and activate the major haemorrhage protocol."

grid.label: Primary survey and escalation
grid.fail: Starts with a pelvic X-ray or secondary survey; no trauma team or senior call.
grid.pass: <C>ABCDE with trauma team; two large-bore cannulas (intraosseous if needed); bloods and crossmatch; activates the major haemorrhage protocol.
grid.high: Uses his physiology and response to fluids to trigger the protocol; calls interventional radiology, orthopaedics and theatres early.

grid.label: Pelvic binder
grid.fail: Places the binder over the iliac crests, or springs the pelvis to test stability.
grid.pass: Applies a purpose-made binder centred over the greater trochanters, feet and knees together.
grid.high: Explains the crest position fails to close the ring; avoids repeated pelvic springing, which can dislodge clot.

grid.label: Tranexamic acid and blood
grid.fail: Omits tranexamic acid or runs litres of crystalloid.
grid.pass: Tranexamic acid as soon as possible, within 3 hours: 1 g over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours.
grid.high: No crystalloid in active bleeding: plasma and red cells 1:1, restrictive resuscitation until the bleeding is controlled.

grid.label: Response decides the next step
grid.fail: Sends him to CT while still hypotensive after blood.
grid.pass: Responder: immediate contrast CT. Non-responder: minimal imaging (chest and pelvic X-ray, FAST) and straight to haemorrhage control.
grid.high: Knows a negative FAST does not exclude retroperitoneal bleeding; non-responder needs angioembolisation or pelvic packing and damage control.

grid.label: Associated injuries
grid.fail: Passes a urethral catheter despite blood at the meatus.
grid.pass: Looks for blood at the meatus, perineal bruising and open wounds; no blind urethral catheter if a urethral injury is suspected.
grid.high: Examines the perineum, rectum and vagina for an open fracture; open fracture needs a general or colorectal surgeon.

grid.label: After stabilisation
grid.fail: Leaves the binder on for days or removes it for an X-ray while unstable.
grid.pass: Post-binder pelvic X-ray once stable, even after a normal CT, because the binder can hide the injury.
grid.high: Binder off ideally within 24 hours; external fixation if definitive surgery is delayed; transfer to the major trauma centre.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: He's just arrived. What do you do?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd get a pelvic X-ray first to see what we're dealing with.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The X-ray shows an open-book fracture.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd spring the pelvis to check, then put a binder round the iliac crests.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Two litres of saline, and I'd leave tranexamic acid for now.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: After 4 units of blood he's still 80 systolic.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd get the CT with contrast now so we know exactly where it's bleeding.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: There's blood at the urethral meatus.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd catheterise to monitor his urine output.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: He stabilises. What about the binder?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Leave it on until the orthopaedic operation next week.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: He's just arrived. What do you do?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Trauma team, catastrophic haemorrhage first, then ABCDE. Two large-bore cannulas, bloods and crossmatch, and activate the major haemorrhage protocol.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How do you apply the binder?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Centred over the greater trochanters, with his knees and feet together.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Tranexamic acid now, as it's within 3 hours: 1 g over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: He's a non-responder. Chest and pelvic X-ray and FAST only, then straight to haemorrhage control. If he had responded, CT.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: There's blood at the urethral meatus.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Suspected urethral injury: no blind urethral catheter. I'd check the perineum for open wounds.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A post-binder pelvic X-ray, because the binder can hide how bad the injury is.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: He's just arrived. What do you do?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Catastrophic haemorrhage and ABCDE with the trauma team. His physiology meets the trigger, so I'd activate the major haemorrhage protocol and call interventional radiology, orthopaedics and theatres now.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Why not put the binder over the iliac crests?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Too high: it won't close the ring. It goes over the trochanters. And I wouldn't spring the pelvis again; it can dislodge clot.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: No crystalloid while he's bleeding. Plasma and red cells 1:1, aiming for a central pulse rather than a normal blood pressure until the bleeding is controlled.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: He's still 80 systolic. FAST is negative.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A negative FAST doesn't exclude retroperitoneal bleeding. He needs angioembolisation for arterial bleeding, or pelvic packing with damage control surgery if he's too unstable.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Anything else on the secondary survey?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Perineal, rectal and vaginal examination: a wound there makes it an open fracture, and I'd call the general or colorectal surgeon.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Binder off ideally within 24 hours; external fixation if definitive fixation has to wait; ongoing care at the major trauma centre.

failures.consequence: He can die in the scanner while bleeding goes uncontrolled.

failures.move: Placing the binder over the iliac crests.
failures.consequence: The ring stays open and pelvic bleeding continues.

failures.move: Giving litres of crystalloid and no tranexamic acid.
failures.consequence: Dilutional coagulopathy and continued fibrinolysis worsen the bleeding.

failures.move: Blind urethral catheterisation with blood at the meatus.
failures.consequence: A partial urethral tear can be made complete.

recovery.line: Let me go back: binder, blood and tranexamic acid first; imaging must not delay haemorrhage control.

recovery.when: Asked about CT in an unstable patient
recovery.line: CT is for the responder; a non-responder goes straight to haemorrhage control.

knowledge.fact: Binder over the greater trochanters, not the iliac crests.
Tranexamic acid as soon as possible; not beyond 3 hours unless hyperfibrinolysis. CRASH-2 dose: 1 g over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours.
Active bleeding in hospital: no crystalloid; plasma to red cells 1:1; restrictive resuscitation until bleeding controlled.
Responder: immediate CT. Non-responder: minimal imaging, then haemorrhage control. Negative FAST does not exclude bleeding.
Interventional radiology for active arterial pelvic bleeding unless open surgery is needed for other injuries.
Post-binder X-ray once stable; binder removal ideally within 24 hours.

recall.think: Exsanguination from the pelvis; a non-responder lost in the CT scanner.
recall.say: "Binder at the trochanters, major haemorrhage protocol, tranexamic acid."
do: Tranexamic acid; plasma and red cells 1:1
Responder to CT; non-responder to haemorrhage control

numbers.meaning: Tranexamic acid not given after this unless hyperfibrinolysis
Plasma to red cells in active bleeding

recall.trap: A negative FAST does not exclude pelvic bleeding.
recall.finish: Angioembolisation or pelvic packing; external fixation; definitive fixation at the major trauma centre.

media.task: Candidate describes the pelvic radiograph and names the injury pattern.
media.description: AP pelvic radiograph of an adult showing an open-book (anteroposterior compression) injury: pubic symphysis diastasis with widening of one sacroiliac joint, no binder in place.

partner.opening: This 34-year-old motorcyclist has just arrived. HR 128, BP 82/50, severe pelvic pain, no binder. What do you do?

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for the pelvic X-ray
reveals.finding: Pubic symphysis diastasis with a widened right sacroiliac joint: open-book injury.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for the response after binder, tranexamic acid and 4 units of blood with plasma
reveals.finding: HR 124, BP 84/52. Still a non-responder. FAST negative.
Blood at the urethral meatus and scrotal bruising. No perineal or rectal wound.
Angiography: bleeding branch of the right internal iliac artery embolised. HR 96, BP 118/70.

push.question: Where does the binder go?
push.expect: Over the greater trochanters, knees and feet together.

push.question: What dose of tranexamic acid, and what is the time limit?
push.expect: 1 g over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours; not after 3 hours.

push.question: He's still hypotensive after blood. Do you send him to CT?
push.expect: No: non-responder goes to haemorrhage control; CT is for responders.

push.question: When does the binder come off?
push.expect: Once stable, after a post-binder X-ray; ideally within 24 hours.

curveballs.prompt: Isn't the iliac crest close enough?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: the binder must sit over the greater trochanters to close the ring.

curveballs.prompt: The nurse wants to catheterise him for urine output.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Not blindly with blood at the meatus; urology opinion and urethral imaging, or suprapubic drainage.

curveballs.prompt: Interventional radiology is 40 minutes away and he is deteriorating.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Damage control: preperitoneal pelvic packing in theatre, with the consultant.
